platforms.title: Tennis Elbow Self-Test: The Chair Lift Sign
platforms.meta_description: You don't need imaging to check for tennis elbow. A simple chair-lift test and a proven exercise routine can confirm it and help start fixing it.
platforms.body_html:
Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is usually a clinical diagnosis — according to OrthoInfo (AAOS) and Mayo Clinic Sports Medicine, doctors typically don't need imaging to confirm it. That means there's a simple, evidence-based way to check it yourself before booking an appointment, and a specific type of exercise that outperforms simply resting the arm.

Why Does the Chair Test Work?

One classic self-check is the chair lift test: stand facing a chair, grip the top of the backrest with your palm facing down (pronated), elbow straight, and try to lift it slightly off the ground. Pain on the outside of the elbow during this motion is a strong sign of tennis elbow, because it loads the exact tendon — the extensor carpi radialis brevis — that's damaged in this condition. A related version, the middle-finger extension test, involves pressing down on your middle finger while trying to straighten it against resistance; sharp pain at the outer elbow points the same way. It's worth noting where exactly the pain sits: tennis elbow causes pain on the outer side of the elbow, while golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) causes pain on the inner side — the two conditions share a similar mechanism but affect opposite tendons, and the self-tests above are specific to the outer-elbow version.

So What Actually Works?

Research summarized by OrthoInfo and clinical trial registries points to eccentric strengthening as the treatment with the best evidence — not rest alone, and not cortisone injections as a first step. Eccentric exercise means slowly lengthening the muscle under load: hold a light dumbbell with your palm facing down, rest your forearm on a table edge, lift the weight with your other hand, then lower it slowly over 3-4 seconds using only the affected arm. A typical starting protocol is 3 sets of 10-15 slow repetitions, done most days.

How Long Before It Actually Improves?

Consistency matters more than intensity here. Case reviews and physical therapy protocols generally describe noticeable improvement over several weeks to a few months of regular eccentric training, not overnight — early studies on eccentric loading showed measurable gains in strength and reduced pain from around the two-month mark. If the exercise itself causes pain that doesn't settle within about a day, that's a signal to scale back the load or repetitions rather than push through it. A short warm-up with gentle wrist circles before starting also makes the movement easier to control.

What Makes It Worse While You're Recovering

Repetitive gripping motions with the palm facing down — wringing out a towel, carrying a heavy bag by the handle, or typing with wrists bent upward — keep loading the same damaged tendon and can slow recovery even while doing the eccentric exercises correctly. Switching a heavy bag to the unaffected arm, keeping wrists in a neutral position at a keyboard, and taking short breaks from repetitive gripping tasks all give the tendon room to adapt to the new loading pattern instead of fighting against constant irritation.

When to See a Doctor Instead

If pain doesn't ease after weeks of consistent home exercise, if grip strength keeps dropping, or if there's numbness or tingling into the hand, that's outside the scope of self-management — a doctor can rule out nerve involvement and consider other options like bracing or physical therapy supervision.

Try it tonight: do the chair lift test once, gently, and if it confirms tennis elbow, start with just one set of the dumbbell exercise tomorrow.
